name: The Inca Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Inca Empire: From Sapa Inca to Yanakuna
period: c. 1438–1533 (from Pachacuti to the Spanish conquest)

tiers.name: The Sapa Inca and the Coya
tiers.you: You are hailed as the son of the Sun, command the armies and the storehouses of the empire, and must win lands of your own, since your father’s estates stay with the rest of his descendants.
tiers.kid: The Sapa Inca ruled the Inca Empire from the city of Cusco, and his people believed he was the son of the Sun.
tiers.rise: The ruler came from the royal family, normally a son of the previous Sapa Inca. When Huayna Capac died around 1527, his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fought a civil war (1529–1532), and in November 1532 the Spaniards captured the victor, Atahualpa, at Cajamarca.
tiers.why: The Sapa Inca, the “unique Inca”, was believed to descend from the sun god Inti and was hailed as the son of the Sun.

tiers.name: Inca nobles
tiers.term: panaqa (royal lineage), Inka, orejones (the Spaniards' name: "big ears")
tiers.you: You belong to a royal lineage of Cusco: you wear the great ear spools and fine cloth of the nobility, keep the mummy of the ruler you descend from, and may lead an army or govern a quarter of the empire.
tiers.kid: Inca nobles wore large ear ornaments, so the Spanish called them “big ears”.
tiers.rise: Rank came by descent from a ruler, through the mother as well as the father. A lineage that backed the losing side in a succession struggle could be destroyed: in 1532 Atahualpa’s generals took Cusco, burned the mummy of Túpac Inca Yupanqui and killed many of his lineage, who had supported Huáscar.
tiers.why: The Inca nobles were the descendants of the rulers of Cusco, grouped in royal lineages (panaqa).

tiers.name: Incas by privilege
tiers.term: incas de privilegio (the chroniclers' Spanish term)
tiers.you: You were born into one of the peoples around Cusco who were granted the rank of Inca: you may wear the Inca headband and serve as an official in the provinces, but you rank below every Inca of royal descent.
tiers.kid: Some peoples who lived near Cusco were given the rank of Inca as an honour, below the royal family.
tiers.rise: The rulers created the order by granting Inca status to whole peoples of the Cusco region; a person belonged to it by birth into one of those peoples.
tiers.why: The chroniclers describe a second order of Incas: the peoples of the valleys around Cusco who were not descended from the rulers but had been granted the rank of Inca.

tiers.name: Curacas
tiers.term: kuraka (curaca), hatun kuraka (great lord), pachaka kuraka (lord of a hundred)
tiers.you: You rule your own people as your forefathers did, but in the Inca’s name: you send him workers and soldiers, pay no labour tax yourself, and may take several wives and travel in a litter.
tiers.kid: Curacas were local lords who ruled their own people for the Inca and sent him workers and soldiers.
tiers.rise: Office passed within a lord’s family, usually but not always from father to son, and needed the Inca’s approval; a superior could appoint a lesser curaca to his post. Rebellion meant death for the lord and, often, deportation for his people.
tiers.why: The curacas were the hereditary lords of the peoples the Incas had conquered, kept in office to rule their own subjects in the Inca’s name.

tiers.name: Priests
tiers.term: willaq umu (high priest of the Sun)
tiers.you: You serve the Sun at one of the state’s temples, make offerings of llamas, cloth and maize beer, and fast without salt or chilli before the great festivals.
tiers.kid: Inca priests looked after the temples of the Sun and the Moon and led the festivals of the year.
tiers.rise: The high priesthood of the Sun belonged to the royal family; the keepers of local shrines came from their own communities.
tiers.why: A large priesthood served the state religion.

tiers.name: Chosen women
tiers.you: You were chosen as a girl and taken to a house of chosen women, where you weave fine cloth and brew maize beer for the state; you must remain chaste, and the ruler may give you as a wife to a man who has served him.
tiers.kid: The “chosen women” were girls picked to live in special houses, where they wove fine cloth and made food for festivals.
tiers.rise: Officials chose girls from the provinces, most of them from families of rank; most chosen women left the house only as wives given by the ruler, and a girl’s family gained standing from her selection.
tiers.why: Each year officials toured the provinces to choose girls of about eight to ten, most of them daughters of curacas and other families of rank, for their looks, skill and intelligence.

tiers.name: Commoners
tiers.you: You farm your share of your ayllu’s land, take your turn at labour service on the state’s fields, its roads or in its army, and are fed by the state while you work.
tiers.kid: Most people in the Inca Empire were farmers and herders who paid their taxes by working for the state.
tiers.rise: A commoner who served well in war could be rewarded with fine cloth or a wife from among the chosen women, and some became overseers of ten or fifty households, a post that was not hereditary. Rebellion could see a whole community deported as colonists.
tiers.why: Most people were farmers and herders living in ayllus, kin groups that held their land in common and traced their descent from a shared ancestor.

tiers.name: Resettled colonists
tiers.you: Your community was moved by order of the Inca to a province far from home, where you must keep your own dress and may never return; for the first two years you lived from the state’s storehouses.
tiers.kid: The Incas moved whole villages to faraway parts of the empire to guard its borders and keep it loyal.
tiers.rise: Communities were moved by order of the state: loyal ones to hold new provinces, rebellious ones as punishment, skilled ones to work for the state; their descendants stayed where they had been placed.
tiers.why: The Incas moved whole communities from their homelands to other parts of the empire, a policy called mitma, and the settlers were known as mitmaqkuna.

tiers.name: Retainers
tiers.you: You left your ayllu to serve a noble household for life, herding its llamas and farming its estates; you owe no labour turns to the community, and all your work belongs to your master.
tiers.kid: Some people served a noble family or a temple all their lives, herding llamas, farming or keeping house.
tiers.rise: The ruler, the nobles and the temples took people from their ayllus as yanakuna, and their children inherited the status; a trusted retainer of the ruler could be raised to office.
tiers.why: The yanakuna were people who had left their ayllus to serve a master full-time and for life: the Sapa Inca, the Coya, the royal lineages and nobles, or the temples.
